https://www.thetimes.com/uk/obituaries/a.title: Sir John Jennings obituary: Chairman of Shell during Brent Spar controversy
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/obituaries/a.subtitle: Leading figure credited with making the company greener who told the oil industry it had to listen to the public
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/obituaries/a.text:
At the 1996 annual meeting of Shell Transport and Trading the chairman, John Jennings, called for a minute’s silence “to pause for quiet reflection in the spirit of reconciliation”. It was six months after worldwide outrage at the execution of the author Ken Saro-Wiwa and nine other Ogoni activists on the orders of the Nigerian president, Sani Abacha. They had been protesting against Shell’s pollution of the Niger Delta, but were found guilty of arranging the deaths of four pro-government Ogoni leaders. Another 19 rebels, then on death row, were not released until after Abacha died in 1998.
The tension in the room at the Queen Elizabeth Hall on London’s South Bank was matched outside, where 200 demonstrators banged African drums and waved banners demanding “Get the Shell out of Nigeria”.
During his four years as chairman, Jennings had become used to regular disruption by environmental, human rights and anti-apartheid groups, and had learnt from painful experience how to take the heat out of difficult situations. He told a petroleum conference that the oil industry had to learn to listen to the public, acknowledge their fears and concerns, and make its case “with persuasive imagery in an acceptable and media-friendly manner”. He added: “Cold facts alone are not enough.”
Jennings believed that, like ice skaters, the industry would be scored separately for technical content and presentation, and would succeed only if it performed well in both. The 1995 Brent Spar oil storage buoy controversy had delivered harsh lessons. After months of hostile media coverage, Shell had been forced by the environmental pressure group Greenpeace to withdraw plans for sinking the redundant buoy in the Atlantic, even though this was agreed to be the most practical solution, and it had been pumped clean years before. But that took no account of the political furore, in which the company was condemned by several European governments. Even worse, from Jennings’s point of view, his U-turn left John Major, the UK prime minister, looking foolish for having supported Shell in the House of Commons and at a G7 summit. Jennings wrote to Major, regretting “the position in which the outcome of this complex issue placed you and your ministerial colleagues”. Major was understood to be furious.
The Times said in 1997: “At its very heart, Shell is a compromise, run by a committee of managing directors, a marriage of hard-nosed Dutch engineers and wheeling and dealing British accountants.” The Brent Spar and Saro-Wiwa episodes clearly prompted a main rethink by that committee, of which Jennings was a prominent member. One of his colleagues, Cornelius Herkströter, said: “We were somewhat slow in understanding that these [environmental and consumer] groups were tending to acquire authority.”
Jennings made valuable contributions to Shell’s green credentials, improving deep-water drilling techniques and biomass technologies to enable lower-carbon energy. In an exchange of letters in the Financial Times with the Body Shop founder, Anita Roddick, he said: “Shell has just completed an important global exercise in listening to people from both inside and outside the company; 14 round-table conferences with more than 300 people from 53 countries engaged in a dialogue about society’s changing expectations of multinationals. This is not a PR exercise but rather a transparent attempt to find out what people really want from all big corporations, not just Shell. I am not pretending it is easy to satisfy the often conflicting expectations which people have of major companies. Rather, a central plank in the dialogue is for everyone concerned to participate in finding a way to a resolution.”
John Southwood Jennings was born in Oldbury, Worcestershire (now West Midlands), in 1937, the son of George Jennings, an electrician, and his wife Irene (née Bartlett). An only child, he was apparently not close to his parents. When he arrived home from school eager to tell his mother he had come second in class at the end of term, Irene replied: “Why not first?”
He attended Oldbury grammar school, now Langley High, and read geology at the University of Birmingham. A Shell research scholarship at the University of Edinburgh enabled him to obtain a PhD before joining the company in 1961. He later became a Sloan fellow at London Business School.
In 1961 Jennings married Gloria Griffiths. They had a daughter, Susan, who lives in France, and a son, Iain, who worked in the oil industry and died in 2023 of complications from dementia. The marriage was dissolved in 1996. The following year he married Linda Baston (née Zetter), who had worked for him in the chairman’s office. Linda and Susan survive him.
Shell first sent him to Oman as a well-site geologist, where he helped to find that country’s first oil reserves. Within seven years he became chief geologist for Shell UK Exploration and Production. He returned to Oman as exploration manager of Petroleum Development Oman, then Shell’s general manager in Turkey. From 1979 he had executive roles in London and the Hague before being promoted to managing director of Royal Dutch Shell Group in 1987 and chairman of the UK arm, Shell Transport and Trading, from 1993.
After leaving Shell, Jennings became a non-executive director of Intelligent Energy, Apple Oil & Gas, the investment bank Robert Fleming Holdings and the Norwegian certification firm Det Norske Veritas, along with other charitable and educational roles. In 1985 he was appointed CBE, four years later becoming Commandeur de l’Ordre National du Mérite (Gabon), and was knighted in 1997.
Jennings and Linda bought and demolished a house near Exmouth in Devon, commissioning the classical architect William Bertram to design and build an elegant replacement while they lived in the staff cottages. “We had no intention of knocking it down when we bought it,” Jennings said, “but the electrics and plumbing were the pits.” They later moved to Guernsey.
He enjoyed flyfishing and shooting, until recently travelling annually to Alaska to hunt salmon, and maintained his fondness for geology. “He was never happier than when he was in the desert somewhere, digging up rocks, getting his hands dirty,” said Linda.
Sir John Jennings, businessman, was born on March 30, 1937. He died on August 29, 2024, aged 87

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Greenpeace settles with Shell over ‘Cousin Greg lawsuit’
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.subtitle: Environmental charity agrees to donate £300,000 to the RNLI after oil and gas major ‘backs down’ over activists’ ship occupation protest
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
A settlement has been agreed between Shell and Greenpeace after the environmental charity occupied one of the multinational’s vessels to protest against its North Sea oil drilling plans.
The campaign group has agreed to donate £300,000 to the Royal National Lifeboat Institute, after the oil major claimed that it had incurred significant costs when six Greenpeace activists boarded a ship carrying a floating production, storage and offloading vessel last year, as it was en route to a shipyard in Norway.
The activists occupied the vessel, which is ultimately intended for use at the Penguins field in the UK North Sea, for 13 days.
Greenpeace had framed the highly-publicised case as an attempt by a major polluter to silence its critics. It nicknamed the case the “Cousin Greg lawsuit” after a scene in the television drama series Succession, where a character threatens to sue the charity. Jesse Armstrong, the writer of the show, donated £25,000 to the campaign group as it defended the lawsuit.
Areeba Hamid, co-executive director at Greenpeace UK, said: “Shell thought suing us for millions over a peaceful protest would intimidate us, but this case became a PR millstone tied around its neck. The public backlash against its bullying tactics made it back down and settle out of court.”
Shell is Europe’s biggest oil and gas group and made a pre-tax profit of $32.6 billion last year. It procured the floating production, storage and offloading facility for use redeveloping the Penguins oil field in the northern UK North Sea. The field is expected to pump 45,000 barrels per day at peak.
The company said that it was “pleased that the dispute has been settled and that a payment in lieu of the costs it incurred can benefit a charity working on safety at sea”, adding: “For Shell, the right to protest is fundamental and has never been at issue.”
The production vessel was loaded on board another vessel, the White Marlin, and was being transported from China to Norway by contractors for Shell when four Greenpeace activists boarded it near the Canary Islands on January 31. Two further activists boarded it while in the English Channel in early February.
Under the settlement, the environmental group will be prevented from carrying out similar actions at or near the Penguins platforms for ten years and from three of Shell’s other North Sea fields for five years.
Greenpeace said it accepted no liability and would pay no money to Shell. It said it would “continue to campaign against Shell including in the North Sea”.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Inside Dale Vince’s messy divorce, from squats to yachts
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Leading Labour Party donor. Former backer of Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion. A caravan-driving new age traveller in the 1980s who became a multimillionaire titan of Britain’s green industries in the 2010s, and the owner of Forest Green Rovers, the world’s first vegan, carbon-neutral football club. Dale Vince is the Richard Branson of renewable energy: flamboyant, outspoken, impossible to ignore.
But in tense divorce hearings at the Royal Courts of Justice last week, Kate Vince, his ex-wife, shone a spotlight on the private life of Britain’s pre-eminent green benefactor, describing Dale Vince, 62, as a man who had “no problem in participating in conspicuous consumerism”.
She told the court on Thursday that he flew in private jets, drank Dom Perignon champagne and bought designer clothing, powerful petrol-powered cars and a luxury 56ft yacht.
Under cross examination on Wednesday from Richard Todd KC, representing his ex-wife, Vince denied that he and Kate had shared a romantic helicopter ride over a Canadian glacier on their wedding day in February 2006.
The expensive lawyers and tales of excessive consumption sit in stark contrast to the life Vince led 40 years ago and the story he has told the British public about his ideals and beliefs.
The son of a Norfolk lorry driver, he spent the 1980s living outside society in a converted ambulance, too poor to buy shoes and eating food taken from rubbish bins.
After dropping out of school aged 15, Vince’s ascent to success began when he rigged a wind turbine to the roof of his campervan at Glastonbury in the early 1990s and used it to charge mobile phones. He founded Britain’s first green energy supplier, Ecotricity, in 1995 and was appointed OBE nine years later. The company’s low-key offices in Stroud are minutes from where he squatted in more indigent times.
In June 2021, when he sold a component business, Electric Highway, the world’s first national charging network for electric cars, to Gridserve, Vince found himself with a huge windfall.
Vince’s properties included Rodborough Fort, an 18th-century folly in Stroud, which he has since given to Kate Vince. His donations to Just Stop Oil and Animal Rising, his bestselling memoir-manifesto and endless media appearances have made him the most prominent environmentalist in Britain after Sir David Attenborough.
His uniform — a half-shaven head, piercings, silver chains and shark-tooth necklaces, black hoodies bearing white skulls, complicatedly distressed jeans and trainers — is that of the self-conscious eco-maverick. Vince looks as though he has just wandered into the television studio or the courtroom after a long morning at a protest drum circle.
He once told the Financial Times: “Business is a sad waste of life, on the whole, and the free market is an oxymoron.” In recent years he has flirted with a run at parliament and spoken about wanting to buy The Observer. His multimillion-pound donations have made him one of the Labour Party’s biggest supporters, alongside the Autoglass magnate Gary Lubner and Lord Sainsbury of Turville.
Vince’s attachment to Labour’s plans for a green jobs revolution led him to switch his support from Just Stop Oil at the end of 2023. “I do want to influence policy by doing the things I do,” he told the Guardian. Whether that will extend to making school dinners across England and Wales vegan — an idea he floated at a fringe event at the Labour conference — remains to be seen.
On Tuesday, the court heard that he had no plans to donate more money to Labour. “I don’t think Labour needs money now,” he said.
It is not his first divorce: in 2016 Kathleen Wyatt, whom he married in 1981 and divorced in 1992 and with whom he had lived a New Age traveller lifestyle in the 1980s, was awarded a “modest” lump sum of £300,000. She had taken legal action in 2011 seeking £1.9 million. Vince spent more than £500,000 fighting the case, saying: “I think it is very wrong just to cash in what is in effect a very old lottery ticket on her part.”
Lawyers for Kate Vince are seeking a 50 per cent share of the couple’s assets, including Ecotricity. The court heard last week that Vince did not want to sell his “life’s work” as a result of the hearings.
Throughout the week, Lewis Marks KC, for her ex-husband, and Todd took turns to question the couple. The top-flight barristers, the acrimonious split and the huge fortune at stake all added to the bristling courtroom drama.
Kate Vince denied that she was using the hearings to humiliate her ex-husband. In October, her barrister told the court that Vince was convinced he would receive a peerage from Sir Keir Starmer’s government and that he was attempting to hasten the divorce so she would not benefit from his potential elevation to the House of Lords. A lawyer representing Vince dismissed the assertion as an attempt to turn the hearing into a “circus”.
Dale and Kate Vince met in 1997 through his firm, the Renewable Energy Company, which evolved into Ecotricity Limited. They became romantically involved in 1999 and married in 2006. They had a son together and split in February 2022. The court was told that after Kate struggled with long-term Covid-related illnesses, Vince announced that he wanted to separate. “He wanted more fun,” she said.
In her written evidence, she said that her ex-husband had “strong ideals”, adding: “I liked meat but Dale said that he would not kiss me if I ate meat. I had to become a vegan.”
She said their lifestyle became more luxurious after 2008 as Ecotricity took off. She recalled a champagne-fuelled trip to Croatia by private jet, and a “cardboard mountain” outside the door of one of their homes that pointed to their scale of consumption. “It was excessive consumerism and we were very much part of it,” she said.
The family wined and dined at the best restaurants, drank expensive champagne and had a regular private driver, she added. The court heard they often flew first or business class and used a private jet on two occasions.
Vince, in his written evidence, maintained that he had tried to live a “low-impact” life since the 1980s, inspired by the concepts of “lower consumption and greater sustainability”.
On Thursday, Marks questioned Kate Vince’s spending after the couple separated. Marks said he had rarely seen such a lengthy inventory of chattels worth more than £500. The court heard that Vince had given his ex-wife millions of pounds since they separated. When Kate Vince could not explain how some of the money was spent, Marks quoted the late George Best to emphasise her heavy spending: “Most of it went on booze and fags and the rest I just wasted.”
When Todd asked Vince what he intended to do in the future, he outlined plans to derive an edible protein source for humans from grass. Other items on his agenda include rewilding projects, the decarbonisation of home heating and building a wooden football stadium for Forest Green Rovers at an estimated cost of £60 million.
Kate Vince, a keen rider, plans to open an equestrian centre for 12 horses.
The hearing is due to conclude this month.
